newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh PM stays home after reported threats.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh PM stays home after reported threats.

text.p: Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina celebrated her 50th birthday in the safety of her home on Saturday after newspapers reported threats to assassinate the recently-elected leader.
"We can't afford to take any threats, real or phony, lightly," one of her aides said.
Police stepped up security in the capital, searching cars and advising Hasina to stay at home and turn away offerings of flowers or other presents.
A popular Bengali-language daily, Ajker Kajog, said in a front-page story on Saturday that "intelligence agents have discovered and foiled another bid to kill Sheikh Hasina."
It said the plot to kill her was made by political opponents who had hired "suicide killers" to act before October 8.
Police said they tightened security in the capital, searching vehicles and looking for anyone acting suspiciously.
Police said they did not know of any particular threat to Hasina's life, which the Ajker Kagoj and other newspapers have reported over the last few days.
"But we will also not simply ignore them," one police officer said.
Officials said they ordered tight security for the prime minister, and advised her to avoid public engagements until October 8 when the incumbent President, Abdur Rahman Biswas, retires.
"Yes, we have asked for a security mop-up. No threat can be taken lightly. She (Hasina) has also been advised not to accept flower bouquets," one official told Reuters on Saturday.
Biswas will be replaced by former chief justice Shahabuddin Ahmed, who was elected by parliament in July for a five-year tenure in office.
Biswas is an active member of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), headed by former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia.

While holding a largely ceremonial position, Biswas surprised Bangladeshis by sacking the army chief, Lieutenant- General Abu Saleh Mohammad Nasina, at the height of political tension in June, accusing him of plotting a revolt.
The newspapers said the transition from Biswas to Ahmed could be an "occasion for trying any upset" for Hasina's three-month-old government.

Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, the man who led Bangladesh to independence from Pakistan in 1971, was killed in a 1975 military coup, followed by the killing of four top leaders of his Awami League in Dhaka Central Jail.
Police recently arrested three former army officers for what they said was their alleged involvement in Mujib's assassination and a possible role in the jail killings.
"They are being investigated," one policeman said on Saturday.
Hasina took over the job of prime minister on June 23 after elections returned the Awami League to power after 21 years, on the eve of the August 15 anniversary of her father's death.
